title: A Spoonful of Peanut Butter Before Bed Could Help You Sleep, Says US Physician
excerpt: Dr Kunal Sood explains the science behind a bedtime habit gaining traction on social media — and why stable blood sugar may be the key to staying asleep through the night.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dr. Kunal Sood recommends peanut butter before bed to enhance sleep quality.
  • Peanut butter contains tryptophan, magnesium, and healthy fats that aid sleep.
  • Healthy fats stabilize blood sugar, preventing cortisol spikes that disrupt sleep.
  • Choose natural peanut butter with minimal ingredients for maximum benefits.

If you find yourself waking up at 3 a.m. for no apparent reason, a US physician says the fix might already be sitting in your kitchen cupboard.

The Instagram Tip Going Viral

Dr Kunal Sood, an American physician, recently shared a deceptively simple piece of health advice on Instagram: eat a spoonful of peanut butter before going to sleep. The tip, which quickly gained traction on social media, rests on a straightforward biochemical argument about blood sugar and sleep architecture.

"It costs nothing, while it can definitely help some people sleep," Dr Sood said, according to a report in the Hindustan Times.

Choosing the Right Peanut Butter
›Opt for natural varieties with just peanuts.
›Avoid added oils, sugar, and artificial additives.
›Unblanched peanut butter has more fiber and antioxidants.
›Portion control is crucial to prevent weight gain.

The Science: Tryptophan, Magnesium and Blood Sugar

The mechanism involves three overlapping pathways.

First, peanut butter is a natural source of tryptophan, an amino acid that serves as a precursor to serotonin — the neurotransmitter associated with calm and relaxation. Serotonin, in turn, is converted into melatonin, the hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle.

Second, the magnesium content in peanut butter supports muscle relaxation and has been linked to improved sleep quality in clinical research. A deficiency in magnesium — common in modern diets — is associated with restless sleep and frequent waking.

"The reason you sometimes wake up at night is because of the peak and the sudden fall in blood sugar."

— Dr Kunal Sood

Third, and perhaps most critically, the healthy fats in peanut butter slow the absorption of carbohydrates, helping to stabilise blood sugar levels throughout the night. When blood sugar drops sharply during sleep, the body responds by releasing cortisol — a stress hormone that raises alertness and can jolt you awake. By providing a slow-release source of energy, a small serving of peanut butter before bed can buffer against these nocturnal dips.

Not All Peanut Butter Is Created Equal

Nutritionists caution that the benefits depend heavily on the type of peanut butter consumed. The recommendation is to choose "natural" varieties with a minimal ingredient list — ideally, just peanuts, with no added oils, sugar, salt or artificial additives.

Commercially popular brands often contain palm oil, hydrogenated fats and high-fructose sweeteners that can negate the very health benefits the snack is supposed to deliver. Unblanched peanut butter — made with peanuts that retain their skins — has been shown to contain higher levels of fibre and antioxidants.

Portion control also matters. A tablespoon of peanut butter contains approximately 90 calories, making it a calorie-dense food. Overconsumption, particularly as an addition to an already adequate evening meal, could contribute to weight gain over time.

A Year-Round Strategy, Not Just a Summer Fix

While Dr Sood's advice gained attention as a summer sleep hack — when heat, extended daylight and disrupted routines commonly interfere with rest — the underlying science applies year-round. Overnight blood sugar stability is a factor in sleep quality regardless of season.

Research published in the Journal of Nutrition found that nighttime peanut consumption in adults with elevated fasting glucose did not worsen blood sugar levels compared with other isocaloric snacks, suggesting the practice is safe even for those managing pre-diabetic conditions. Separate studies have shown that higher protein intake before sleep may support muscle recovery and improve overall sleep architecture.

For the millions of Indians in the diaspora juggling demanding work schedules, late-night calls across time zones and the stress of distance from family, a simple, accessible sleep intervention carries particular appeal — provided it comes from a jar with nothing but peanuts on the label.
